inline.s: At the University of California, Berkeley, there was a gymnast named Dan

Millman. From a very young age he loved gymnastics and enjoyed watching others practice it, so he joined the gymnastics team while still very young. He was very talented and extremely diligent; except for attending classes, eating, and sleeping, he spent all day practicing gymnastics in the gymnasium. For there was only one purpose in his life: to win an Olympic gold medal.

It was also because of gymnastics that he entered UC Berkeley, where he spent all day practicing together with the members of the gymnastics team. Before the Olympics there was always a qualifying competition, the National Collegiate Championship; whoever won it would represent the United States at the Olympics. Among all the gymnasts, he was the one the coaches of the whole school regarded most highly.

Later, in the year just before the competition, he had an accident: while riding his motorcycle he collided with a car, was flung through the air, and broke his right leg. After six months of rehabilitation, he returned to the gymnastics team. But when he practiced gymnastics, he felt his strength failing him, and he could no longer perform at his former level. So his teammates gradually distanced themselves from him, and the coach told him: You have no hope now; you must leave the gymnastics team for good and seek another path.

He was utterly dejected, for since childhood he had set his heart on winning an Olympic gymnastics gold medal. So at night he would often wake from nightmares; the accident had wounded him too deeply, destroying the ideals and aspirations of his whole life, and even his will to live had entirely collapsed.

One night he suddenly woke from a nightmare and could not fall back asleep, so he went out for a walk. As he walked, he came upon a gas station open at night, where an old man was filling gas for others. He walked over and asked: ‘Don’t you get very tired, filling gas all day like this?’ The old man said: ‘Not at all — I’m serving people, and it makes me very happy!’ After finishing with a customer, the old man chatted with the young man: ‘You don’t look like you’re in a very good mood.’ He said: ‘That’s right! Ever since I was injured, I haven’t been able to perform at my level, so I’m very downhearted.’ The old man said: ‘Then let it go for now! You have nothing to do at the moment, so why not come and fill gas with me? While we serve others, we can chat along the way.’ Because the young man’s spirits lifted every time he finished talking with the old man, the two became friends.

One day, as he was about to leave, the old man said: ‘Bring your hiking shoes tomorrow morning; I’ll take you to a very beautiful place, and you’ll be delighted when you see it.’ Because the young man was in a very low mood, on hearing that there was a beautiful place he was very happy and full of expectation. The next morning he brought his hiking shoes, and the old man took him mountain climbing, the two of them chatting and laughing all the way. They climbed for three hours and reached the summit. After reaching the top, the young man said: ‘Hey, weren’t you going to take me to see something beautiful?’ The old man said: ‘The beautiful thing is right here before you.’ So the young man looked down at the ground — a stone! He picked it up and said: ‘Just this stone?’ And with that, he threw it away.

The old man said: ‘Why are you so frustrated today?’ He went on: ‘You! You care too much about the result!’ He said: ‘I told you I would take you to a beautiful place. Look — all the way here the two of us chatted happily and enjoyed so much scenery. With each climb, the view kept changing. Yet in the end you saw only one stone! You picked it up and threw it away. It is just like your pursuit of an Olympic gold medal: you win the medal, and still you will lose it — like the stone, the result is something that will be lost. You win the Olympic gold this time, and next time it will be taken by someone else; you will still lose it!’ He added: ‘Since you love gymnastics, you should treat gymnastics as the tempering of your life, not as the pursuit of a gold medal. The crux of your problem is that your mind weighs gain and loss too heavily, thinking only of the result while neglecting the process. You should use this condition of gymnastics to train your inner concentration and endurance, and take it as an ideal and aspiration for your life. Do not mind how the outer circumstances are; treat it as a self-perfecting of your life. Use gymnastics to put into practice your inner perfection, and manifest your inner perfection through every movement. Remember, desire will make you suffer and keep you from doing things well, and life will become a burden and a struggle.’

After hearing this, the young man had a sudden awakening. After he went back, he continued to practice gymnastics, but his state of mind was completely different. At that time he did not dare practice with the others; he would slip into the gymnasium secretly after everyone else had left class. But by now he no longer wanted the gold medal. He let go of all thoughts of gain and loss entirely, and concentrated on every movement, using that one thought of the mind to observe and to feel, living in the present within each movement. He progressed faster and faster. In the end, movements he had been unable to perform before — for example, jumping down and doing three somersaults before landing — he could now do.

Later, at the time of the formal competition, the coach would not let him take part. He said: ‘Coach, stand over there, and I’ll perform for you.’ As soon as he went up, everyone was stunned. Not only had his performance not declined because of the injury; it was even better than before. Later he competed in UC Berkeley’s competition and won UC Berkeley’s championship, then represented UC Berkeley in the National Collegiate Championship and won the national collegiate championship.
